In a sense, yes. The internationally oriented afrobeats is often just pop music on a beat with some log drums. The success that some artists have had with this is definitely influencing some artists to pursue this sound.

However, I don't really think at this point afrobeats is losing its local identity. I think the way the Western music industry has pushed this specific sound has also served to insulate the industry. Sure, we have more artists experimenting with new sounds but that's just how music works - artists and producers experiment and inspire others. That doesn't really make it any less of a local identity. 

Hard to specifically address this since I think it's easy to argue that, today, afrobeats is just an umbrella term and not really a genre. But some genres commonly considered afrobeats that I think are really pushing the sound forward and not at all losing local identity but perhaps reflecting evolutions in local identity/values are afro-adura, alté (which we could also say is just an umbrella term at this point), and fujipiano.

text:
I listened to Twice As Tall by Burna Boy, which was submitted by u/1Afrokid. I liked it! It was pretty entertaining hip hop record. One thing that's different about this and a standard hip hop album I guess is the foreign language that is used sometimes (though most of the album is still English), and I'm not entirely sure what it is, but it sounds cool. I admit I don't know much about the languages spoken in Nigeria but what I can say is that I always enjoy songs that aren't in English. It's an entirely different sound set and it's always intriguing to me to find the differences in how the singing sounds. It's a whole new world of possibilities. My only criticism is that a lot of the songs end up sounding pretty similar and generic. A good example for this is No Fit Vex, which is the only song I didn't like, not because it's bad but because it's uninspired and steals ideas from other songs from the album. There's some good stuff here, so I don't believe that's the best he could make. The album itself is pretty minimalistic, there's not much happening at any given time. That's not a criticism, it's a stylistic choice that I appreciated. It made the album really calm and vibey. Not like what the cover art suggested, which is pretty grandiose. Speaking of the cover art, if this guy is from Nigeria, why are Egyptian pyramids and the Sphinx in the background? I find that odd. The artwork is great but it doesn't fit the album at all imo. Well, let's talk about those good songs then, shall we? Bebo was a pretty whacky song but I was digging it. It's one of those earworm songs that are annoying on paper but they're really fun to listen to. Wonderful was great too. I loved the choral effect but that's not surprising coming from me. The same applies to Time Flies, which has like an a capella band as guest vocalists and they were awesome. Overall, this is my favourite song and the instruments seem more involved here as well, which for me is a plus always. Monsters You Made was one of the most unique songs. The guest singer is great and the chorus is catchy. Great job on picking a guest vocalist again. Well that's pretty much it, there were some other fun songs like Way Too Big, but overall it was a really nice album, if only generic at times. I feel like there's a lot of room for improvement and this one stayed in its comfort zone a bit too much but I hope he'll make more experimental albums because the tracks that did break the monotonity were amazing.

Songs I particularly liked: Way Too Big, Bebo, Wonderful, Comma, Time Flies, Monsters You Made

Songs I wasn't crazy about: No Fit Vex

I just want to quickly mention that I've created a [Spotify playlist](https://open.spotify.com/playlist/6UeVmURYhWyOVcT6yawRM3?si=664ec6d902dd4ac5) for this project, where I've added all of the albums I've so far listened to. Keep in mind that it's not a complete list, because not all of the albums were on Spotify, but most are there, so feel free to follow it if you want.

Ok so my general feedback is there is a lot of potential here. Your voice is really powerful and beautiful and can carry a lot of emotion with it. Standouts to me in a good way are the Daughter portion of Who Am I / Daughter, Feet On Ground, Indigo, Gbam, and Iroko. I think leaning into these sounds more would really benefit you.

Where I think there is a lot of improvement is in vocal texture and your hooks. You definitely would benefit from more variation in vocal texture, especially within songs. It sounds like for the most part, on each song you have chosen one way to sing and carry that throughout. While the talk/rap parts might be an effort to add some variation here, I think they were genuinely poorly executed, and I'm not sure they really fit well with your strengths. This should really be evaluated as to how they could be better or, honestly, whether you should even continue doing that. And then the hooks, I just think they are mostly not effective. They aren't really adding anything to any of your songs, and a lot of the times the connection between the hooks and verses are just not really evident.

But again, overall, I think you did some really great things here and that you have a lot of potential. Honestly for an album with 11 songs, there are five I really did like which is very good. I would recommend you listen to Qing Madi, specifically the I Am the Blueprint album - I think you have a lot of similarities in your vocals, but the way she varies the way she uses her voice is something to study for you.

Below are my live reactions/feedback to the songs as I listened through.

LOVE start of the intro track. I'm hoping the vocals are you because the voice is nice. The speak-singing though... I think it can work but there's something off. Maybe mic quality? I'm hearing like some sort of weird noise at the end of hard consonants. Overall Baba Mi was okay, but could be an excellent intro to a cohesive project so I will assume that's what it is because I heard a lot of good things and really like your voice.

Who Am I / Daughter - Damn when you get to the part where you're speaking to your daughter, that part is incredible and powerful. The Who Am I portion lost me a bit like I got the idea but I think you dove too quickly into the reflection part. Some more details on the experience that led to those reflections would have improved the message imo. Also the talk/rap part honestly isn't really helping the song at all - would say it took away from a beautiful song. imo the Daughter part should stand alone.

Iya - I don't think this is the right sound for your vocals. Your vocals are so powerful and I think this song is hiding that. And, again, the talk/rap part doesn't sound right - it sounds forced. I'm not sure what it is specifically, but I would suggest evaluating how you incorporate that and work on your delivery. It's pretty weak as it is, especially when contrasted with your vocals. This song felt a bit like filler, like the vocals weren't really hitting the way they did in the first two songs.

Feet On Ground - I like this a lottttt. I think it's really great up until you do the talking part. I won't keep harping on it, but I think it's not really fitting in well with your music, and it's very distinctly less powerful than your vocals. This song kinda has a Ghana afrobeats vibe too, I like it. Probably my favorite complete song so far.

Pepper - This song is okay but I feel it has a bit of a dated vibe to it. It's pretty forgettable to me, ngl. Just sounds like the type of song a lot of artists make when they're trying to make a hit but it just sounds too much like everything else. I feel like I've heard variations of this song countless times.

Ase - Similar feedback to Pepper. I hope this isn't too harsh but it reminds me of when Western artists try to make afrobeats. I don't think your vocals are right for this type of song at all. 

Indigo - I really like this one. It's really well done, it's powerful, it has a really captivating feel to it, it makes me want to move, and the lyrics are solid.

Palm Wine - This starts out really nicely. But I think it starts feeling a bit flat as you get to the middle of the song. The hook is a bit boring and would benefit by being better connected to the song - like I understand the connection, but it feels separate, if that makes any sense. I don't really know how to explain this better.

Gbam - This whole time I was feeling like you're missing variance in vocal texture. But I think you do a decent job of it here. I really like this one. Actually I love it. Beautiful song, you do a great job at create a whole atmosphere here. It's just a lovely song. Not sure why you put the live session immediately after, though. Should be at the end imo as sort of a bonus track or something like that.

Victor - The vocal texture issues are back. It just kinda drones on and no part of the song is capturing my attention. It's not bad, just kinda dull imo.

Iroko - Love how this song puts your vocals at the forefront, and the instrumentals are awesome. Love this vibe. Again, I think more variation in vocal texture would make this better.

text:
It absolutely is an umbrella term, but it also definitely has overarching commonalities. I'm not really so familiar with music theory but as someone who has exposed myself to a very wide range of music, and actively try to listen to a wide range of genres but really have gravitated more and more to the umbrella genre known as afrobeats, I think there are still aspects of afrobeats music that do set it apart. Also, limiting afrobeats to Nigeria only is the only thing you said here that I can say is definitively incorrect, and it can even be argued the umbrella genre really originated directly from the evolution of hiplife in Ghana. Also, I don't know if you can really put afro-swing into the afrobeats genre - while it has afro beats elements, I think it is arguably closer to dancehall, which also does have significant cross-influences with afrobeats.

From my perspective, some things that define afrobeats for me include:

* Bouncy beats - Sub-genres of afrobeats have vastly different sounds but I think what really does tie it together is that the beats have something of a bounce to them. I think it very much does come from permutations of the 5-beat pattern.
* Inclusion of local languages, especially pidgin. In this respect, I think geography/ethnicity does play a role in defining the umbrella term. But I think this has become very much an integral element of afrobeats - and it is something that, as the genre grows in the West beyond the diaspora, makes people get the false sense that afrobeats is all about dancing just because they don't at all or don't fully understand the lyrics, especially when they hear familiar English words used in ways that don't necessarily make sense to them in pidgin.
* Call-and-response hooks. I think this is something that is sometimes overlooked, and is something really cool that I think is being put into afrobeats music even more explicitly over the past few years (I think it has been a common theme throughout but was done less explicitly, and obviously is a major element of Afrobeat music). A lot of traditional West African music involves call-and-response and I think this is a part of afrobeats that really gets fucked up in the Westernised mimicry of afrobeats and also is virtually non-existent in, for example, afro-swing.
* Emotionality. Contrary to what virtually every person I have discussed Afrobeats with who is not of African descent, the music is lyrically quite penetrating. If you listen to how the music is sung, I think it is uniquely driven by emotion that fully immerses the listener into the songs. As a genre, I think, as a rule, it does an incredible job at conveying human emotion and is uniquely vulnerable - even the songs that are aimed at "flexing" typically touch upon the challenges associated with wealth and fame (I know, so sad so so sad lol). But I think unlike many other genres, a heavy emphasis is placed on conveying human emotion and less on storytelling.
* Use of proverbs, especially modern-day proverbs. I think people tend to overlook what is happening in the now and romanticise the past. They will even claim that the repetitive use of phrases in afrobeats is a lack of originality. However, Afrobeats is rich with common phrases that both reflect and influence modern-day lexicon including the use of specific modern-day proverbs, which is a key part of how afrobeats in my opinion is hugely important for preserving culture, especially protecting the genre from the gentrification imposed on it at times by Western labels and the allure of the money that can come in from the Western music industry.

This honestly is just a start and a bit of stream of consciousness. It's kinda something I have been wanting to write down for a while now so thank you for providing me with the exact right questions at the right time for this to happen. I know people may disagree with what I've said here as well, so happy to hear alternative perspectives on this too :)
